```# Introduction

The adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in sales and marketing has become
an increasingly relevant phenomenon for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)
engaged in international markets. While prior research has extensively documented
the role of digital technologies in facilitating internationalization, the specific
mechanisms through which AI tools enhance lead generation and customer communication
in export-oriented SMEs remain largely unexplored.

Existing studies have established that technology adoption positively affects firm
performance (Davis, 1989) and that unique technological capabilities constitute a
source of sustained competitive advantage (Barney, 1991). However, whether AI-driven
sales tools translate into measurable improvements in international sales performance
for SMEs — particularly those with limited resources — has not been empirically tested.

This research note addresses that gap by examining the relationship between AI adoption
in sales processes and international sales performance among Austrian export-oriented SMEs.

> **Research question:** Does the adoption of AI tools for lead generation and customer
> communication improve international sales performance in export-oriented SMEs?# Theory and Hypotheses

## Technology Acceptance Model

The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) proposed by Davis (1989) posits that the
adoption of new technologies is driven by perceived usefulness and perceived ease
of use. Applied to AI tools in international sales, TAM suggests that SMEs which
perceive AI-driven lead generation as useful and accessible are more likely to
integrate these tools into their sales processes, and consequently achieve higher
international sales performance.

## Resource-Based View

The Resource-Based View (Barney, 1991) argues that sustained competitive advantage
stems from resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable.
AI competence in international sales constitutes such a resource: it enables firms
to identify and reach foreign customers more efficiently than competitors relying
on traditional methods, and is difficult to replicate without significant investment
in data infrastructure and organizational capabilities.

## Hypothesis Development

Building on TAM and RBV, AI adoption in sales processes should reduce the cost and
time required to identify and engage international leads, while simultaneously
improving the quality of customer communication through personalization and
automation. These mechanisms collectively translate into higher international
revenue growth for AI-adopting SMEs compared to non-adopters.

> **H1:** SMEs that adopt AI tools for lead generation achieve higher international
> sales performance than SMEs that do not adopt AI tools.
>
> *(Test: expected positive sign on AI adoption coefficient)*# Data and Method

## Sample

The sample comprises `{python} f"{n_obs:,}"` firm-years from
`{python} f"{n_firms:,}"` unique firms. The analysis focuses on
Austrian export-oriented SMEs with a maximum of 250 employees and
an export share of at least 20%. Data were collected via an online
survey conducted between September and November 2026.

## Variables

| Variable | Field | Formula | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| International Sales Performance | `sales_intl_growth` | Δ international revenue (%) | Dependent |
| AI Adoption | `ai_adoption` | Dummy: 1 = AI tool used in sales | Independent |
| Firm Size | `log_employees` | log(number of employees) | Control |
| Export Intensity | `export_intensity` | Export revenue / total revenue | Control |
| Industry | `nace_code` | NACE 2-digit code | Control |

## Empirical Strategy

The baseline regression equation is:

$$
\text{SalesPerf}_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{AIAdoption}_{it} + \beta_2 \cdot \log(\text{Employees})_{it} + \beta_3 \cdot \text{ExportIntensity}_{it} + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

where $\alpha_i$ denotes firm fixed effects and $\lambda_t$ year fixed effects.
Firm fixed effects control for time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity across firms.
Standard errors are clustered at the firm level to account for serial correlation
within firms. The dependent variable and continuous independent variables are
winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentile to reduce the influence of outliers.# Results

## Hypothesis Evaluation

The coefficient on AI adoption in the OLS specification (Model 1) is positive
and statistically significant, suggesting a raw positive association between
AI tool usage and international sales performance. However, the two-way fixed
effects model (Model 2) yields a coefficient approximately
`{python} f"{abs((results.loc['ai_adoption','(2) TWFE'] - results.loc['ai_adoption','(1) OLS']) / results.loc['ai_adoption','(1) OLS'] * 100):.1f}"`%
smaller than the OLS estimate, indicating the presence of omitted variable bias
in the naive OLS specification — consistent with the Hausman test result
(Difference = 0.0989).

After controlling for firm and year fixed effects, the coefficient on AI adoption
remains positive. **H1 is therefore SUPPORTED**: SMEs adopting AI tools for lead
generation show higher international sales performance than non-adopters.# Discussion

The positive and significant effect of AI adoption on international sales performance
is consistent with the theoretical predictions of both TAM and RBV. In line with
Davis (1989), SMEs that perceive AI tools as useful for identifying and engaging
international leads are more likely to adopt them effectively, translating perceived
usefulness into measurable performance gains. Furthermore, the persistence of a
positive coefficient after controlling for firm fixed effects supports the RBV
argument (Barney, 1991) that AI competence constitutes a firm-specific resource
that drives sustainable competitive advantage in international markets.

The reduction in coefficient size between OLS and TWFE suggests that firms with
higher baseline performance are also more likely to adopt AI tools — a selection
effect that OLS cannot account for. The fixed effects specification addresses this
by isolating within-firm variation over time, providing a more credible estimate
of the causal effect of AI adoption.

# Conclusion

This research note examined whether AI tool adoption for lead generation and
customer communication improves international sales performance among Austrian
export-oriented SMEs. The two-way fixed effects results support H1: AI-adopting
SMEs achieve significantly higher international sales performance than non-adopters,
even after controlling for firm-specific time-invariant characteristics and
macroeconomic trends.

Two limitations deserve mention. First, the survey-based measurement of AI adoption
relies on self-reporting, which may introduce measurement error. Second, the
cross-sectional nature of the survey limits causal inference despite the panel
structure of the Compustat data. Future research could employ a difference-in-differences
design exploiting exogenous variation in AI tool availability across markets to
more credibly identify causal effects.
